cards.title: Denmark Data Breach Exposes 8.8M People's Personal Data

depth.text: someone misused a **Danish company's legal access** to expose personal details for **8.8 million people**

The exposed data included **names, addresses and CPR numbers**. A review found that names and addresses of people with name-and-address protection were not included. The CPR administration has **stopped the company's access** and is working with specialists and authorities to map what happened.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters say organizations can't be trusted with people's data and want penalties for breaches; others hope the incident will lead to stricter security and say CPR numbers should be treated as usernames, not passwords.

cards.title: We ported the original Doom to SQL

depth.text: someone ported **Doom**'s game logic and renderer to **SQL**, and got multiplayer working too

The game logic and renderer run as **SQL queries** inside a database; Python handles timing, keyboard input, and displaying the bitmap. The game loop runs at **35 FPS**, while the renderer can produce frames at up to **60 Hz**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some see SQL as a useful place for complex business rules; others call the game-logic approach engineering malpractice, even while loving the stunt.

comments.text: > I was surprised how easy it is to express pretty complicated game logic in SQL. The game logic is just ~5900 lines of SQL. cards.title: Self-hosted HTTP tunnels with SSH and Nginx

depth.text: someone built a **self-hosted tunnel** for sharing **local web previews** using software already on their server

The author uses OpenSSH to get a **free remote port**, then nginx routes a matching subdomain to the forwarded service. A **signed link** can expire, but the article warns that anyone with the secret could reach **any TCP port** listening on 127.0.0.1 or 0.0.0.0.

cards.camps: Two camps: some like reusing existing tools and self-hosting; others call this setup over-complicated and risky, or say a normal home server is enough.

comments.text: A number of years ago, I created a fully open source (MIT) project called sish [0] that does just this. sish is a SSH server written specifically for tunneling. You can tunnel websockets, TCP connections, and even have…

Ideally we end up with solutions like this that can be run entirely without an…

depth.text: someone found a **compiler bug** in Infidel that quietly **overwrote the game's memory**

ZIL mistook the **global variable's index**, 30, for its value, so the routine wrote from address 30 instead of the array at 11129. With enough objects, it could overwrite the **abbreviations table** and garble the game's text.

depth.text: someone shared photos of a **beautiful old control room** that once managed electricity for **Southern Rail**

Built during **1936**, it was one of five control rooms for the Southern Rail network, with panels linked to substations at different locations. Two on-site engineers could rapidly reconfigure the electricity flow after faults, but still had to **wind up the switchboard** to use the telephone. It remained in use until **1997**, when a new substation took over most of its tasks.

comments.text: Misread the title as "Working" control room, and was ready to be amazed that something like that from the first half of the last century was still in use... and not even a PC or screen to be found. But, it was decomissioned in 1997. Really interesting how depression-era infrastructure like that was still built with so much attention to aesthetic design. Today it would just be screens on a wall…

It's great that so much about those old control rooms is posted here lately! One thing I notice is how much efforts had been spent to illustrate both the current status of the system, but also it's overall structure and how the two relate - i.e. the actual components of the facility. Almost all of the dashboards here have some kind of graph, showing the wiring or plumbing between components, or…

There's something very beautiful about the attention to detail and forethought that has gone into rooms like this. The wonderful combination of beauty through a clear focus on functionality, supported by just enough of a sense of majesty to lift the whole space beyond pure functionality makes it a little more special. This is probably a place that was always considered at least somewhat beautiful…
If, like me, you were wondering what the room /actually/ looks like: https://www.flickr.com/photos/132123913@N03/albums/721577110...

cards.title: Improper redaction reveals Google Data Center water and electricity usage

Agate LLC reported **52.65 megawatts** at peak electrical demand and **13.299 megagallons** of water. Across six reporting data centers, the article says water use totaled **765 million gallons** last year; Papillion’s Fireball Group LLC reported 547.88 megagallons.
data: Six reporting data centers' water use

cards.camps: Two camps: some call the Lincoln site's water use insignificant next to farming; others say data-center water use and missing disclosure remain worth scrutiny.
entities: Nebraska Department of Water, Energy, and Environment

So a single average Nebraska farm uses roughly 30 times the water the…

Excited to give this a try once it’s ready!

Runescape was the first thing that got me into coding. Fell in love with the game and had a ton of admiration for the devs who could spend decades crafting the same game, to create such a wonderful playground for so many millions of people. Stopped playing after a few years but still have many fond memories of the joy I had everyday after school logging onto that game.
For anyone unaware this is stated to essentially be the MMO continuation of Runescape Dragonwilds which was a survival and crafting game that recently released into 1.0 after its commercial success.

Initially, I misread the headline as referring to RuneQuest, the Betamax of tabletop fantasy role playing. Better than D&D, but which didn't win the popularity contest. It is one of three games I would love to see made into software, with the other two being Traveller and Paranoia (the computer is your friend, trust the computer)

I learned programming writing Runescape Macros in Pascal and later Java. Honestly still enjoy writing automation today because of it, I've gotten to use a lot of the skills I learned from OG RS at work.
